analysis.one_liner: Adds a prescription drug benefit to Medicare, delivered through private insurance plans.
analysis.headline: The Medicare drug benefit bill passed the House by one vote (220-215), passed the Senate 54-44, and became law on December 8, 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: This law created Medicare Part D, the first federal program to help pay for prescription drugs for older and disabled Americans. It pays for the drug coverage through private insurance plans rather than directly through Medicare, gives the government no authority to negotiate drug prices, and bars cheaper drugs from Canada. It also shifted more Medicare patients into private health plans, created tax-advantaged Health Savings Accounts, and included many payment increases for hospitals, doctors, insurers, and drug makers.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries who lack drug coverage gain a new benefit to help pay for prescriptions, with larger subsidies for low-income seniors and people with high drug costs. Private insurers, pharmacy benefit managers, and drug manufacturers gain a large new federally funded market delivered through their plans, and hospitals and physicians gain payment increases in the same law.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a new voluntary Medicare prescription drug benefit (Part D) starting January 1, 2006, for all Medicare beneficiaries regardless of income or health status, with low-income enrollees receiving full premium subsidies and reduced cost-sharing.
The standard benefit includes a catastrophic cap: after a beneficiary pays $3,600 out of pocket in 2006, Medicare covers nearly all remaining drug costs for the year.
Transitional discount cards and up to $600 in assistance for low-income beneficiaries begin within about six months of enactment, before the full benefit starts in 2006.
Adds new Medicare coverage for an initial physical exam, cardiovascular screening blood tests, and diabetes screening tests.
Increases Medicare payments to rural hospitals, rural physicians, rural ambulances, and home health agencies, and raises physician payment updates.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers fund the new drug subsidies and higher provider payments. Beneficiaries pay premiums, a $250 deductible, 25 percent coinsurance, and full drug costs in a coverage gap, and higher-income beneficiaries pay more of their Part B premiums. The law bars Medicare from negotiating drug prices and blocks drug importation, keeping drug prices high for beneficiaries and taxpayers.

drawbacks.text: The standard benefit had a gap in coverage: after costs reach the $2,250 initial coverage limit, the beneficiary pays the full cost of drugs until out-of-pocket spending reaches $3,600, leaving millions to pay full price in the middle of the year.

Medicare is barred from interfering with negotiations between manufacturers and plans and may not require a formulary or a price structure, so the government cannot use its bargaining power to negotiate drug prices.

Although the law directs the Secretary to allow drug importation from Canada, implementation was conditioned on a determination that it would pose no additional risk to public health and safety and would reduce costs, which effectively prevented it from taking effect.

The drug benefit is delivered through private plans that bear financial risk, with federal subsidies and reinsurance flowing through them, locking private insurers and pharmacy benefit managers into a permanent middleman role in the new public benefit.
Beneficiaries with incomes above $80,000 ($160,000 for couples) pay higher Medicare Part B premiums beginning in 2007, an income-test of the premium subsidy.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The law delivers a real, previously nonexistent federal drug benefit to millions of seniors, with strong protections for the poorest beneficiaries. But it was designed so that the money flows through and to private insurance plans and pharmacy intermediaries rather than directly through Medicare, and it deliberately leaves the government without authority to negotiate drug prices or to import cheaper drugs from Canada — provisions that keep drug costs higher for both beneficiaries and taxpayers than they otherwise would be. Its designers protected industry interests on pricing while providing an expansion of benefits to ordinary people that was genuinely large.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 220-215, the Senate passed it 54-44, the President signed it, and it became Public Law 108-173.

narrative.text: The House passed the bill by a recorded vote of 220 to 215, with 1 present.
The Senate had passed its own drug bill (S.1) earlier, and the House-Senate conference negotiated a compromise version of the prescription drug benefit.
In the Senate, the conference report passed 54 to 44.
President Bush signed the bill, and it became Public Law 108-173, the Medicare Prescription Drug, Improvement, and Modernization Act of 2003.

At least sixteen separate motions to instruct conferees — motions telling House conferees to negotiate for specific changes such as allowing drug importation or requiring Medicare to negotiate — were offered by House Democrats and all failed on party-line votes.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Seniors gained a new drug benefit; private insurers, drug manufacturers, and pharmacy benefit managers gained a permanent, federally funded marketplace for their services.

sides.party_line_note: Passage was sharply partisan: 207 of 229 House Republicans and 16 of 205 House Democrats voted yes in the House, and 42 of 51 Senate Republicans and 11 of 48 Senate Democrats voted yes in the Senate.

industries.industry: Private health insurers and Medicare Advantage plans
industries.note: The law requires the new Medicare drug benefit to be delivered through private prescription drug plans and Medicare Advantage plans, which also receive federal subsidies, reinsurance, and risk-corridor protections, making private insurers permanent intermediaries in Medicare. Insurers also gain new managed-care payment rates set at least as high as traditional Medicare.

Drug companies gain a large new pool of customers paying with federal subsidies, while the law prohibits Medicare from negotiating prices or requiring formularies and effectively blocks cheaper drug importation from Canada, keeping drug prices high for beneficiaries and taxpayers.

Because the drug benefit runs through private plans that negotiate drug prices as intermediaries, pharmacy benefit managers gain a central role in the new program; the FTC is directed only to study differences in pharmacy payment under PBM plans.

The law raises Medicare payment updates for hospitals, physicians, home health agencies, ambulances, and rural and critical access hospitals, and adds new preventive service coverage, increasing payments to providers serving Medicare beneficiaries.
The law creates Health Savings Accounts, allowing tax-deductible contributions to pay medical expenses, giving banks and insurers new products and giving higher-income taxpayers a new tax shelter.
The law freezes payment updates for durable medical equipment and moves to competitive bidding in large metropolitan areas, reducing payments to some suppliers while adding quality standards.
